name: Oaxaca
tagline: Street-cart tlayudas, artisanal mezcal, and a terrace with a view of Santo Domingo.

Casa Oaxaca.description: An iconic terrace with a view of the Santo Domingo temple, a reference for contemporary Oaxacan cuisine.

Mezcaloteca.description: An artisanal mezcal tasting room, a serious introduction to the region's mezcals.

Tlamanalli.description: Traditional Zapotec cooking from the Mendoza family in Teotitlán del Valle, with corn ground by hand by chef Abigail Mendoza. Anthony Bourdain visited on 'Parts Unknown.'

Lechoncito de Oro.description: A street stand for pork tacos and tortas, next to the Mercado 20 de Noviembre.

Levadura de Olla.description: Chef Thalia Barrios García honors the recipes of San Mateo Yucutindoo in a colonial courtyard. Mentioned in the Michelin Guide.

Criollo.description: A UNESCO-heritage colonial house where chef Enrique Olvera (of Pujol) and Luis Arellano serve a daily tasting menu built around local, seasonal ingredients, with tortillas made to order over wood-burning ovens. Featured on the World's 50 Best Discovery platform.

Origen.description: Oaxacan chef Rodolfo Castellanos, winner of Top Chef Mexico, has reinterpreted the state's traditional cuisine with contemporary technique since 2011, with dishes like crab paella and mole-glazed duck confit.

Pitiona.description: Chef-driven tasting cuisine from José Manuel Baños, trained at El Bulli and Arzak, served in a restored house with a rooftop terrace overlooking the seven main churches of the historic center.

Los Danzantes.description: A restaurant with more than two decades of history in a colonial courtyard next to Santo Domingo, producing its own mezcal to pair with mole and contemporary Oaxacan dishes.

In Situ Mezcalería.description: A reference mezcalería near the zócalo with one of the city's most extensive and carefully curated mezcal lists, recognized on the World's 50 Best Discovery platform.

Sabina Sabe.description: A mezcal and cocktail bar named after Mazatec healer María Sabina, with drinks built around local ingredients; featured on World's 50 Best Discovery.

Itanoni.description: A tortillería and antojería founded in 2001 by Amado Ramírez Leyva devoted to preserving native varieties of Oaxacan corn, hand-ground for memelas, tlayudas and tetelas. Listed in the Michelin Guide.

Boulenc.description: A bakery and café known for naturally leavened breads, croissants and international dishes served in a covered courtyard; a favorite stop for food critics visiting Oaxaca.

Las Quince Letras.description: Chef Celia Florián's restaurant, open since 1992, celebrated for its mole tasting flight, especially a smoky mole negro. Awarded the Michelin Guide's Bib Gourmand distinction in 2024, 2025 and 2026.

Catedral.description: An Oaxacan institution since 1976 a block from the zócalo, set in a colonial mansion, serving mole, chiles rellenos and squash-vine soup in a classic setting.

La Biznaga.description: A relaxed restaurant with an open-air patio on García Vigil, serving contemporary Oaxacan cooking alongside a solid mezcal selection.

Zandunga.description: Isthmus flavor in central Oaxaca: it grew out of the weekend meals Aurora Toledo used to cook and formally opened as a restaurant in 2002, serving garnachas and mezcal cocktails.

La Teca.description: More than 30 years serving the hearty cuisine of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, with stews, seafood and garnachas prepared by Isthmus-born cooks.

El Destilado.description: A project by chefs Julio Aguilera, Jason Cox and Joseph Gilbert, alumni of San Francisco's Saison, offering tasting menus of chef-driven Mexican cuisine alongside an extensive mezcal list.

Almú.description: Wood-fire 'cocina de humo' in San Martín Tilcajete, just outside the city, serving memelas, enmoladas and tlayudas cooked over an open flame; recognized in the Michelin Guide.

Alfonsina.description: Chef Jorge León, trained at Casa Oaxaca and Pujol, cooks in honor of his grandmother Alfonsina in San Juan Bautista La Raya; featured on World's 50 Best Discovery and in the Michelin Guide.

Casa Crespo.description: A restaurant, cooking school and chocolate shop run by chef Óscar Carrizosa, offering a seven-mole tasting flight served over heirloom-corn tortillas and paired with mezcal.

Mayordomo.description: A chocolate shop founded in 1956 by Salvador Flores in Tlacolula, using a formula of just four ingredients (roasted cacao, sugar, almonds and cinnamon); one of Oaxaca's best-known chocolate and mole brands.

Mercado 20 de Noviembre.description: A market built in 1882 whose 'smoke corridor' concentrates dozens of grilled-meat stalls — tasajo, cecina, chorizo — eaten with fresh tortillas amid the smoke of the grills.

Mercado Benito Juárez.description: A traditional market a block from the zócalo selling chapulines, tejate, tlayudas and regional sweets; a local culinary ritual for more than a century.

Tlayudas Libres.description: A night stand with more than 50 years of history on Calle de los Libres, considered the original 'tlayudas de Libres', open from 9pm into the early morning.

Café Brújula.description: A local specialty-coffee chain founded in 2006 with direct trade ties to growers' cooperatives in Oaxaca's Sierra Sur, including the 'Mujeres Voladoras' blend produced entirely by women.

La Casa de la Abuela.description: With more than 25 years overlooking the zócalo and the Cathedral, it serves the most classic Oaxacan cooking, including four kinds of mole (negro, amarillo, coloradito and almendrado).

El Mesón Oaxaqueño.description: A classic restaurant on a corner of the zócalo specializing in tlayudas, mole and mezcal, popular with both locals and visitors.

Memelas Doña Vale.description: Valentina 'Doña Vale' Hernández's memela stand in the Central de Abastos market, with more than 30 years of history; her memelas with asiento, beans and quesillo were featured in Netflix's 'Street Food: Latin America'.

Marco Polo.description: A seafood restaurant with a decades-old garden patio, serving shrimp and brick-oven fish, a Oaxacan classic for breakfast or lunch.

La Cocina de Humo.description: Chef Thalía Barrios García's second restaurant, recreating a traditional Sierra kitchen with comal, metate and ancestral cooking techniques; featured on World's 50 Best Discovery.

La Olla.description: Two blocks from Santo Domingo, chef Pilar Cabrera has run this restaurant for more than 20 years, serving Oaxacan and continental cooking along with vegetarian options.

Txalaparta.description: A mezcal and craft-beer bar with a rooftop terrace, relaxed at sunset and a dance floor by night; a regular stop on the city's mezcal-bar circuits.

Los Pacos.description: An emblematic restaurant founded in 1985 by Francisco Canseco and 'Doña Soco', known for its tasting flight of the seven traditional Oaxacan moles, now run by Laura Canseco Florián.

La Popular.description: A simple local café on García Vigil, a favorite among Oaxacans for its good-value home cooking and friendly service.

Terranova.description: A restaurant with more than two decades under the zócalo's arcades, featuring live mariachi music; Anthony Bourdain stopped here during his Oaxaca visit on 'Parts Unknown'.

Nieves de la Soledad.description: Facing the Basílica de la Soledad in the Jardín Sócrates, several artisanal ice-cream stands have been making nieves since 1930, with more than 50 flavors including leche quemada and hoja santa.

Cafeto & Baristas.description: A tiny three-table café two blocks from Santo Domingo, focused on coffee from the Oaxaca Coast and manual brewing methods since 2014.

Los Tacos de Esme.description: A family-run hole-in-the-wall taquería in the Santa María del Marquesado neighborhood, with tortillas, fillings and salsas made to order; highly recommended by local Oaxaca taco guides.
